newsitem.title: FRANCE: TENNIS-TEAM SPIRIT PROPELS FRANCE AND SWEDEN TO DAVIS CUP FINAL.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-TEAM SPIRIT PROPELS FRANCE AND SWEDEN TO DAVIS CUP FINAL.

text.p: Team spirit rather than individual flair has propelled Sweden and France to the Davis Cup final in Malmo next month.
Each country has two players in the top 20, Cedric Pioline and Arnaud Boetsch for France and Thomas Enqvist and Stefan Edberg for Sweden.
On paper, both teams are weaker individually on clay than the Americans, Germans and Spaniards and would not have been tipped to qualify for the final.
"In some countries, the Davis Cup is a tradition which amounts for players to playing a grand slam final," said French national coach Patrice Hagelauer.
"Team events rely heavily on values such as comradeship and solidarity. These values have a boosting effect on some players."
In France, Boestch was at his best this season in the Davis Cup while in Sweden Magnus Larsson has made his name as a result of the event.
In both countries public funding and state intervention is a tradition. Sports bodies have launched extensive youth programmes and local authorities have assisted tennis clubs.
In Sweden, Bjorn Borg's successes in the late 1970s and early 1980s spurred the tennis federation into action.

"Tennis really boomed in popularity after Bjorn and tennis halls sprang up everywhere. You only have to look at our results to see what it has meant for us," federation chairman Anders Wetterberg said.
Local authorities provided land and financial guarantees to the thousands of private tennis clubs across the country seeking to breed a new generation of champions.
A population of just eight million has almost 120,000 families registered as tennis club members and no fewer than 12,000 licensed competition players.
In France, by contrast, the lack of a big tennis name has started a trend.
France had a hugely popular event, the French Open, but no players to win it.
A state funded system was launched in the 1970s, helping clubs spot talented young players and setting up tennis high schools all over France in which youngsters train as well as study.
The most gifted end up in the Tennis National Centre, based at the Roland Garros stadium, site of the French Open.
Team spirit is fostered by a host of team competitions between the 9,000 clubs who possess 500,000 licensed players.
As a result, France this year won the European under-14 championship and the under-16 World Cup.
"Cedric Pioline is a very good example of the situation," said Hagelauer.

"For four years he refused to play the Davis Cup. It is no wonder he is the only player in the French team not to have come out of the federation system and not to have played these youth team competitions."
But Hagelauer said the detection would be even better had sports a bigger say at school.
"In Sweden, sport takes a much bigger place at school than in France. It certainly helps, too," he said.

The results speak for themselves. Apart from the seemingly endless list of Swedish victories in major tournaments, the country's Davis Cup team will be hoping to clinch their sixth victory in their 10th Cup final next month.
Sweden's harsh winters rule out outdoor training for six months of the year, so most of the country's 765 tennis clubs have built indoor facilities.
Consequently, Swedes have tended to fare better on hard surfaces than on grass, with Stefan Edberg the notable exception.
